title: Comprehensive Single-Cell Chromatin and Transcriptomic Profiling of Peripheral Immune Cells in Non-Segmental Vitiligo.
abstract: INTRODUCTION Non-segmental vitiligo (NSV) is an autoimmune condition characterized by melanocyte loss. While skin-specific mechanisms are well-studied, systemic immune dysregulation contributing to NSV pathogenesis remains unclear. OBJECTIVE This study employs a multi-omic single-cell approach to investigate circulating immune cells in NSV, integrating transcriptional and chromatin accessibility data. METHODS An integrative scRNA-seq/scATAC-seq analysis was conducted on PBMCs from NSV patients (n=11) and controls (n=5), identifying transcriptional markers, cell-cell interactions, chromatin accessibility, and transcription factor (TF) dynamics. Key findings were validated in an expanded cohort (NSV, n=16; controls, n=9) using spectral flow cytometry, with additional stratification by sex, age, disease activity, severity, and duration. RESULTS Analysis of 59,192 PBMCs identified 8,204 gene expression markers and 13,925 ATAC peaks across 25 immune cell subtypes. A broadly activated immune response was observed, characterized by cytotoxicity, antigen presentation, cell exhaustion, and stress, predominantly in monocytes, NK cells, CD8+ T cells, and dendritic cells (DCs). Multi-omic integration revealed Th1/Th17 polarization and dysfunctional regulatory T cell (Treg/mTreg) responses. Chromatin accessibility highlighted enriched TF binding sites for FOXO3, SP1, AP1, STAT1/STAT3, IRF1, and IRF4, regulating pathways linked to cytotoxicity, antigen processing, NF-κB, Toll-like receptor, and JAK-STAT signaling.Flow cytometry validated these findings, showing that disease activity and shorter duration were associated with heightened immune dysregulation. Robust TCR activation drove Th1/Th17 polarization and elevated IFN-γ and TNF-α production in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. CLA+ skin-homing Th1/Th17-polarized CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and mTregs exhibited persistent activation, marked by basal PD1+ expression. OX40/OX40L-mediated interactions between monocytes and effector T cells amplified inflammation. Regulatory dysfunction, including reduced IL-4 and IL-13 production in mTregs, was prominent in moderate-severe and active disease. CONCLUSION This is the first multi-omic single-cell study in PBMCs of NSV patients, revealing systemic immune dysregulation driven by cytotoxicity, antigen presentation, exhaustion, and regulatory failure. Disease severity, activity, and evolution influence these pathways, highlighting the OX40/OX40L axis as a potential therapeutic target to mitigate immune dysregulation and relapse risk.

title: Proteomic Identification of Plasma Proteins Associated with Future Dementia Development
abstract: Dementia is a progressive decline of cognitive abilities, severe enough to affect daily life activities and independent function. Dementia is most common in older individuals: about one-third of adults 85 years or older may exhibit Alzheimer disease (AD) related dementia, but it is not a normal part of aging (1). Various neurodegenerative disorders contribute to the development of dementia through progressive and irreversible loss of neurons and brain function. AD accounts for 60%–80% of dementia cases (1). Amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles are key pathological features of AD. Amyloid beta 42 and p-tau are known biomarkers for the presence of AD pathology and therapeutic targets (2). However, these AD biomarkers do not appear to be well suited on their own for determining the risk of developing AD dementia before amyloid pathology or related cognitive symptoms appear. Furthermore, therapies targeting these pathologies have shown modest but not complete clinical improvement of cognitive symptoms. While our knowledge regarding biomarkers for AD and other dementias has increased dramatically in recent years, a better understanding of biological pathways that may lead to development of dementia, and the identification of potential associated biomarkers, may enable the selective application of preventive measures including therapeutic interventions and lifestyle changes. Current known risks for dementia include, but are not limited to, nonmodifiable factors such as age and genetics. For example, the risk of AD dementia and vascular dementia increases with age; while the most significant genetic risk factor for sporadic AD is the presence of the apolipoprotein E gene APOE4 (3). The reason APOE4 increases AD risk is not well understood and inheriting APOE4 does not ensure on its own that the individual will develop AD. Modifiable risk factors of dementia include smoking, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease (4). AD is characterized by a long asymptomatic preclinical phase in which the individuals appear to be cognitively normal (CN) but have evidence of amyloid pathology (2). However, many CN individuals presenting with amyloid pathological changes never develop AD dementia using current cognitive assessments. This further highlights the need to identify new biomarkers and therapeutic targets for long-term dementia risk stratification and disease progression. One way to achieve this is by employing proteomic methods to retrospectively identify proteins that are differentially expressed in individuals who developed dementia versus those who do not. While proteomic studies have been undertaken to identify potentially clinically relevant proteins, most previous studies have focused on identifying risk factors in individuals in a time frame relatively close to disease onset. Walker et al. undertook a multifaceted approach to identify relative plasma protein abundance associated with the development of dementia in individuals 45 to 65 years of age, often decades prior to the development of dementia related symptoms (5). In a primary proteomic discovery analysis, 1784 individuals who developed dementia over the course of a 25-year follow-up period were retrospectively identified out of 10 981 participants in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Community study cohort. This provided a large cohort for SomaLogic’s SomaScan v.4 proteomic analysis utilizing 5284 nucleic acid-based protein binding aptamers to query the association of the abundance of 4877 plasma proteins with long-term neurocognitive outcomes. However, some potential drawbacks of aptamer-based biomarker discovery include overrepresentation of secreted proteins, cross-reactivity with nonintended target proteins, and target protein affinity variations related to protein complexing or single nucleotide polymorphisms. Using this initial proteomic analysis, a total of 32 proteins were associated with future development of dementia (Table 1). After adjusting for known risk factors (APOE4 status, cardiovascular disease, and kidney dysfunction), 26 proteins were found to be associated with the development of dementia within 25 years. Seven proteins were found to be associated with the development of dementia within 15 years as determined by an internal replication study on the original study cohort. Only one protein, Growth/Differentiation Factor-15 (GDF-15), was found to be associated with dementia risk in both the 25-year and 15-year groups. Further work was then performed to better elucidate the potential clinical relevance of the 32 proteins identified by the initial proteomic analysis. Two independent secondary study external replication cohorts were used to attempt to reproduce the association of the discovered proteins with dementia development and to evaluate their association with known CSF biomarkers of AD pathology, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation. Fifteen of the 32 originally identified proteins were associated with the development of dementia in at least one of the 2 replication cohorts via SomaScan abundance assessment of 4877 proteins. To assess for potential differential protein expression in brain tissue of AD patients, some (but not all) protein expression patterns in post mortem brain tissues versus control brain tissues were examined in 2 patient cohorts. Eight unique proteins, denoted as + in Table 1, were identified to be differentially expressed in AD patient brain tissue as compared to control brain tissue in at least one cohort. Additional studies were conducted to evaluate the expression of the identified proteins in brain tissue, to assess the biological pathways and protein networks linked with the identified proteins, and Mendelian randomization analysis and genome-wide association studies to assess association with AD, and plasma protein abundance. While these various studies did not uniformly indicate association of all proteins with dementia, several proteins were associated with CSF markers of AD (amyloid beta and p-tau) and/or associated with non-AD specific markers of neurodegeneration (including total-tau and neurofilament light chain). Four of the identified proteins are prioritized AD therapeutic targets; 8 proteins are targets of non-AD existing drugs; and 3 of the proteins have been genetically linked to AD (Table 1). The protein that exhibited the strongest association with 25-year dementia risk was GDF-15, but this immune and stress response protein does not appear to be linked to an AD specific role and was not associated with CSF amyloid and/or p-tau concentrations. This extensive analysis identified 4 potentially overlapping functional pathways, previously known to be associated with long-term development of dementia: proteostasis, immunity, synaptic function, and extracellular matrix organization (ECMO). Fifteen of the 32 originally identified proteins were classified as “prioritized midlife biomarkers of dementia risk and AD” and placed into one of the 4 functional pathways by the authors (see Table 1). While the degree of risk associated with these proteins and associated pathways for the development of dementia is not currently fully understood, these results may spur further investigation into mechanisms that lead to dementia development. For example, the authors suggest a causal relationship for dementia development for the immune-related proteins serpin family A member 3 (SERPINA3) and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), as well as an association of alteration of the extracellular matrix organization related metalloproteinase proteins such as MMP12 and MMP19, with long-term AD risk. Two synaptic proteins appeared to function as midlife markers of AD-related dementia (cerebellin 4 precursor (CBLN4) and glutamate ionotropic receptor delta type subunit 2 (GRID2)). The proteostasis-related proteins such as the heat shock protein heat shock protein family A (Hsp 70) member 1B (HSPA1B), and the chaperone proteins DNAJ Heat Shock Protein Family DNJB9/DNAJB12, were associated with long-term AD dementia risk and the authors suggest that up-regulation of these proteostasis proteins may occur in response to the presence of protein misfolding before the development of dementia. Using a subset of 13 of these proteins, the authors developed a predictive model for the development of future all-cause dementia. This model only achieved a ROC curve (AUC) of 0.66. This predictive model significantly underperformed when compared to a predictive model that included a combination of known risk factors (such as age, APOE4 status, cardiovascular risk factors) with an AUC of 0.77 in the patient cohort. Combining both predictive models did not improve the performance of either model alone. This data indicates that while the identified proteins may be altered in individuals developing dementia later in life; at present they do not represent strong long-term prognostic biomarkers. Furthermore, the remaining challenges in the predictive power of the long-term markers is evident in comparison to the clinical performance of emerging CSF and circulating biomarkers for the evaluation of the presence of amyloid-related pathology, which often exhibit AUCs >0.90 (2). The impressive amount of evidence generated by Walker et al. will require future effort to fully understand and confirm the relevance of their findings to dementia risk and AD pathogenesis, as many of these proteins have some function unrelated to neurological-specific processes. It should be noted that dementia in the original proteomic cohort was not specific to AD and may have been related to other types of dementia or mixed dementias. Furthermore, SomaScan aptamer technology does not detect all potential proteins within the proteome, and indeed, a newer version of SomaScan (not utilized in this study) has expanded the number of protein abundance targets to 7288. However, it is comforting that proteomic analysis did identify multiple proteins previously identified of pathological/therapeutic interest in AD. While this study yielded novel information regarding biological pathways that may lead to dementia development, it remains to be determined as to how these proteins and pathways might lead to the development of dementia much later in life. Further examination of these proteins and pathways may eventually (but not immediately) translate into advances in targeted early intervention. title: Role of STAT1 signaling in development of heart failure post chronic kidney injury
abstract: Clinical trials show that individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD), have a higher risk of heart failure (HF). In our swine model of CKD (renal microembolization), proteomic analysis of left ventricular tissue revealed STAT1 dysregulation in CKD compared to control (WT) swine. STAT1 functions as a central inflammatory mediator activated by type I interferons and various pro-inflammatory cytokines, which are elevated in CKD as a consequence of kidney injury. Once activated, STAT1 drives the expression of genes involved in inflammatory and immune responses[1][2], and may thereby play a central role in HF development in CKD. To investigate the impact of STAT1 signaling CKD induced cardiac dysfunction. CKD was induced by ischemia-reperfusion injury of the left Kidney at the age of 8 to 11 weeks in Transgenic Stat1 Knockout (Stat1-/-) mice and WT Mice. After 1 and 3 months, cardiac ultrasound was performed and left ventricle (LV) and kidney tissue were processed for histology (Picrosirius Red staining), while Bulk RNA transcriptomic analysis was performed in LV myocardium. In addition, the effect of STAT1 inhibition (Fludarbine) on contractile performance was assessed in cultured human myocardial slices. Renal Ischemia reperfusion injury induced chronic kidney disease (CKD) characterized by pronounced renal fibrosis compared to the contralateral kidney, as visualized by Picrosirius Red staining, that was not different between WT and Stat1-/- mice (A, B). Echocardiographic analysis revealed diastolic dysfunction as evidenced by a trend toward increased E’/A‘ ratio (E) and prolonged isovolumetric relaxation time (IVRT) (F) in Stat1-/- mice. RNA sequencing of cardiac tissue identified CKD-induced alterations in multiple signaling pathways, incl the JAK-STAT pathway in WT but not Stat1-/- mice (C). Conversely, Stat1-/- mice, CKD induced a distinct immunological and inflammatory gene expression profile in the heart (D). In human living myocardial slices, STAT1 inhibition with Fludarabine resulted in significant downregulation (around 20%) of contractile performance. Our results emphasize a pivotal role of STAT1 in mediating cardiac responses to chronic kidney disease. Loss of STAT1 profoundly alters the cardiac inflammatory transcriptome and is associated with early diastolic dysfunction and increased macrophage infiltration. These findings position STAT1 axis as a potential therapeutic target in cardiorenal syndrome. Future studies using advanced imaging techniques and functional analysis with the living myocardial slices can further elucidate the underlying mechanisms and support clinical translation.For image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.

title: The management of heart failure: a brief look into the future
abstract: Heart failure (HF) is a major cause of death, hospitalization, morbidity, and cost, with a global prevalence of more than 65 million persons. In Western countries, HF is the most common diagnosis for hospitalization in persons ≥ 65 years. With the development of new therapies which extend the survival of patients with HF and with the ageing of the general population, this prevalence is likely to continue to grow. Thus, HF remains a serious worldwide problem. Fortunately, it is being addressed in preclinical and early clinical studies that are reviewed briefly in this article. Genetic studies have shown that DNA is damaged in mice with HF induced by aortic constriction and an insulin-like growth factor binding cytokine is released by senescent vascular endothelial cells. A vaccine-based molecule against this cytokine ameliorated the cardiac dysfunction, raising the possibility in the future that the development of HF might be reduced by a vaccine in patients at high risk.1 Transthyretin amyloidosis is now recognized more frequently than heretofore to be a cause of a cardiomyopathy that is often fatal. In a Phase 1 study using CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, a single infusion of an investigative drug resulted in striking reductions in serum transthyretin amyloid, suggesting that this serious myopathy may be controlled2; a Phase 3 trial is currently underway. The expression of another gene (BINi) is often reduced in patients with HF, and a trial in patients with chronic HF administered this gene using an adeno-associated viral vector is likely. The circulating messenger (m) RNAs of other genes has been combined to create genetic risk scores which are likely to be of benefit in patient management.3 Although the genetics of HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) are still obscure, the combination of five mRNAs may identify patients at high risk of developing this condition has been described. This could alter clinical management and improve clinical outcome. Metabolomic profiling: It has been observed that the proteome is a strong predictor of mortality in patients with HF, regardless of left ventricular ejection fraction.4 Increased plasma ketone concentrations are associated with enhanced cardiac output and reduced pulmonary arterial wedge pressure. The mechanism of these important actions may be related to providing additional ‘fuel’ to the failing heart and/or reduction of systemic vascular resistance. Indeed, ketogenesis appears to play an important role in the salutary effects of SGLT2 inhibitors,5–7 and orally administered ketones may prove to be beneficial in the management of patients with HF. With new assays, thousands of plasma proteins can now be measured accurately and rapidly. Using machine learning, a small fraction of these are predictors of early mortality which will personalize the care and outcome of patients with HF. Obesity is a chronic disorder that increases the likelihood of the development of HFpEF. Approximately one-third of patients hospitalized for HFpEF in the USA present with central obesity. It is likely that oral glucagon-like protein agonists (GLP-1), probably combined with other potent anti-obesity medications, will play an important role in the prevention and management of HFpEF. Cell therapy for HF has undergone multiple preclinical and early Phases 1 and 2 trials; the former have shown that the injected cells have only a brief life in the myocardium and that any benefit observed may be of pleiotropic origin.8 Among the various cell types that have been studied, autologous pluripotent stem cells and bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells appear to be the most promising. Although a single delivery of these cells may provide modest benefit, preclinical studies have demonstrated that deliveries repeated at intervals enhanced this benefit. This observation may not be practical clinically if the cell delivery must be made into the heart.8 It has also been suggested that intact cells may not be necessary to get these effects. Cell products such as specific mRNAs and microRNAs may be angiogenic and/or anti-apoptotic. If that proves to be the case, it could have a profoundly beneficial effect in the future management of HF. Devices: Cardiology became a distinct specialty at the end of the 19th and the beginning of the 20th centuries by the development of three non-invasive devices: the measurement of arterial pressure, electrocardiography, and cardiac size (by roentgenography). Subsequently, cardiac catheterization, pacemakers, prosthetic heart valves, and heart-lung machines are among the devices that have greatly enhanced the specialty. Attention is now focused on the development of new devices designed to augment the action of drugs in the prevention and the reduction of the severity of HF. They fall into two categories—implanted and wearable.9 Three implanted devices have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for the management of chronic HF. The CardioMEMS system of implantable monitors provides continuous pulmonary artery pressure remotely. This can guide pharmacologic therapy and thereby enhance survival and HF hospitalization in patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).10 Cardiac contractility modulators (CCM) consist of an implanted power source that delivers non-excitatory biphasic electrical impulses to the inter-ventricular septum during the brief refractory period following ventricular contraction,11 These stimuli enhance myocardial contractility by increasing intracellular calcium concentration and/or modifying myocardial gene expression and thereby improve HF patients’ functional capacity and maximal O2 consumption (VO2) and the quality of life in patients with HFrEF. The third approved device in chronic HF is barostimulation in which electrical stimulation of the carotid sinuses increases parasympathetic activation and reduces sympathetic activation, thereby also enhancing ventricular function.12 Intermittent occlusion of the superior vena cava by a balloon mounted on a catheter may be of benefit in patients with acutely decompensated HF.13 Stimulation of the vagus and phrenic nerves and/or of the diaphragm is currently being studied and may prove to be effective in patients with advanced HFrEF. In preclinical studies, a novel transaortic pulsatile pump placed in the descending aorta has undergone encouraging results to unload ventricular function in pigs in cardiogenic shock. While these devices may be effective, they occasionally cause infection or malfunction and are quite costly. However, it is likely that their continued improvement will reduce the threshold for their application in patients with HFrEF, whose symptoms cannot be controlled by medical therapy. It is likely that non-invasive monitoring and telehealth will play increasingly important roles in patients with HF, especially in rural areas. In addition to the information provided by electrocardiography and remote measurement of arterial oxygen saturation, of physical activity (and plasma concentration of glucose in patients with T2D) will be employed more frequently and will be helpful in the determination of the need for adjustment of therapy, of personal visit to a health care facility, or of hospitalization.14 Two additional approaches could have enormously salutary effects in reducing the frequency and severity of HF. The first, for asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic persons, consists simply of much stricter application of established guidelines for primordial and primary care.15 The second, for patients with advanced HF and a serious prognosis, is xenotransplantation of a genetically modified porcine heart, since availability of human donor hearts is inadequate. This approach requires further efforts designed for inhibiting rejection. Between these two ends of the spectrum of HF, the many advances summarized above are likely to improve the future management of patients with this important condition. title: Systematic profiling of subtelomeric silencing factors in budding yeast.
abstract: Subtelomeric gene silencing is the negative transcriptional regulation of genes located close to telomeres. This phenomenon occurs in a variety of eukaryotes with salient physiological implications, such as cell adherence, virulence, immune-system escape, and ageing. The process has been widely studied in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, where genes involved in this process have been identified mostly on a gene-by-gene basis. Here, we introduce a quantitative approach to study gene silencing, that couples the classical URA3 reporter with GFP monitoring, amenable to high-throughput flow cytometry analysis. This dual silencing reporter was integrated into several subtelomeric loci in the genome, where it showed a gradual range of silencing effects. By crossing strains with this dual reporter at the COS12 and YFR057W subtelomeric query loci with gene-deletion mutants, we carried out a large-scale forward screen for potential silencing factors. The approach was replicable and allowed accurate detection of expression changes. Results of our comprehensive screen suggest that the main players influencing subtelomeric silencing were previously known, but additional potential factors underlying chromatin conformation are involved. We validate and report the novel silencing factor LGE1, a protein with unknown molecular function required for histone H2B ubiquitination. Our strategy can be readily combined with other reporters and gene perturbation collections, making it a versatile tool to study gene silencing at a genome-wide scale.

title: Metabolic Regulation of Longevity by One-Carbon Metabolism and Flavin-Containing Monooxygenase
abstract: Abstract Nematode flavin-containing monooxygenase-2 (fmo-2) is induced by dietary restriction and hypoxia, and is required for the longevity and health benefits of these pathways. It is also sufficient to confer these benefits when overexpressed. As FMOs are well-conserved across taxa, the fmo-2 mechanism has high translational potential. To determine the changes that occur following fmo-2 induction, we performed RNA-seq and untargeted metabolomics analyses. Our data reveal that one-carbon metabolism (OCM) is significantly altered by fmo-2 overexpression. OCM is a nexus for essential metabolic pathways, including transmethylation, transsulfuration, nucleotide synthesis, and amino acid metabolism. We hypothesized that fmo-2 confers longevity benefits by altering key metabolic processes within or downstream of OCM. To test this, we asked whether fmo-2 and OCM interact to regulate longevity by knocking down expression of genes involved with OCM and measuring lifespan and oxidative stress resistance. To understand the biological implications of these interactions, we generated a computational model using qPCR data of key OCM-related genes to predict changes in OCM metabolic flux. Our model predicts significant changes in OCM flux that are regulated by fmo-2 expression levels and are consistent with our RNAi and multi-omics results. We are now testing this model by knocking down genes downstream of OCM to determine their role in fmo-2-mediated benefits. Preliminary results support our hypothesis that changes in metabolic flux through OCM are involved downstream of fmo-2 expression, and may also implicate the UPRER in this pathway. Our future work will elucidate this mechanism and link stress perception and fmo-2-mediated longevity.

title: Tissue- and Sex-Specific Molecular Signatures of Aging and the Impact of Developmental Programming
abstract: Abstract Aging, even in healthy individuals, induces a wide range of molecular changes in cells, tissues and organs, resulting in (and mediating) the age-related decline in health. Many of these changes are influenced by both genetic and lifestyle factors, including early exposures during fetal development. We have used baboons, a non-human primate species highly similar in genetics, physiology and nutrition to humans, to characterize age-correlated molecular changes in organs and tissues using in integrated multi-omics approach. We have demonstrated that different organs show early age-related changes at different timepoints, and in a sex-specific manner, highlighting differences in aging and age-related changes to molecular and cellular functions. Also, early molecular changes are tissue-specific, with different genes, proteins, metabolites and pathways affected. Examining the adult offspring born to mothers that are either under-nourished or over-nourished during pregnancy, we also have evidence that these early exposures substantially alter the aging trajectory, lead to different molecular and pathway changes on the cellular level, and result in unique characteristic age-related changes in organ function. This suggests that developmental programming (the exposure in utero) not simply accelerates aging, but fundamentally alters the molecular mechanisms mediating age-related effects in these animals.

title: Integrated multi-omics analysis revealed the molecular networks and potential targets of cellular senescence in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Cellular senescence (CS) is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, the mechanisms through which CS contributes to AD pathogenesis remain poorly understood. We found that CS level in AD was higher compared with the healthy control group. Transcriptome-based differential expression analysis identified 113 CS-related genes in blood and 410 in brain tissue as potential candidate genes involved in AD. To further explore the causal role of these genes, an integrative mendelian randomization analysis was conducted, combining AD genome-wide association study summary statistics with expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) and DNA methylation quantitative trait loci (mQTL) data from blood samples, which identified five putative AD-causal genes (CENPW, EXOSC9, HSPB11, SLC44A2, and SLFN12) and 18 corresponding DNA methylation probes. Additionally, integrative analysis between eQTLs and mQTLs from blood uncovered two genes and 12 corresponding regulatory elements involved in AD. Furthermore, two genes (CDKN2B and ITGAV) were prioritized as putative causal genes in brain tissue and were validated through in vitro experiments. The multi-omics integration study revealed the potential role and underlying biological mechanisms of CS driven by genetic predisposition in AD. This study contributed to fundamental understanding of CS in AD pathogenesis and facilitated the identification of potential therapeutic targets for AD prevention and treatment.

title: L26/P-776 A mendelian randomization study of ovarian aging through the cross-tissue brain-gut-ovary Axis
abstract: Abstract Study question Whether methylation abnormalities, epigenetic regulation, transcription/translation levels (eQTL/pQTL) have a causal relationship with the age of menopause, and cross-tissue effects (e.g., the brain-gut-ovarian axis) . Summary answer Genes IFI16 and PDCD6IP regulate menopausal age through multi-level modulation, Ovarian aging is driven by a cross-tissue genetic network involving the brain, gut, and ovaries. What is known already Age of ovarian failure onset is strongly influenced by genetic factors. Recent studies have shown that the timing of menopause also exhibits unique methylation differences. As a core component of the follicular microenvironment, ovarian granulosa cells may directly influence the age of menopause by regulating the rate of follicular atresia through epigenetic regulation (e.g., DNA methylation) and gene expression dynamics (e.g., eQTL/pQTL). The brain-gut axis, a bidirectional communication system between the gut and the brain, can directly affect ovarian health and even lead to premature ovarian failure and series of reproductive dysfunction issues. Study design, size, duration This study aims to elucidate the genetic mechanisms driving menopausal age by innovatively integrating multi-omics data of ovarian/granulosa cell-related genes (cis-eQTL, mQTL, pQTL), combined with Mendelian randomization (SMR) and co-localization analysis (PPH4>0.8), and utilizing GTEx brain/intestinal tissue eQTL for cross-tissue validation.The blood SNP-CpG association was extracted from the meta-analysis of mQTL by The GoDMC (http://mqtldb.godmc.org.uk/downloads) to identify cis-mQTLs of genetic variants closely associated with ovarian and granulosa cell-related genes. Participants/materials, setting, methods The eQTL data were from the eQTLGen Consortium .The pQTL data were from Egil Ferkingstad et al study. The eQTL data for 14 brain tissues; eQTL data for 3 intestinal tissues were from tissue specific eQTL data. Menopausal age dataset were from ukb-b-17422. A p-value of 5.0 × 10−8 was set for filtering. Coloc R package and STRING used for analysis. The confidence level was 0.15 and PPI score was 0.4. ggplot2 and cytoscape used for visualization Main results and the role of chance 257 ovarian genes (121 risk factors, 136 protective factors) while 11 granulosa cell genes (5 risk factors, 6 protective factors) were associated with menopausal age. 24 ovarian genes have protein association (11 risk factors, 13 protective factors). 152 CpG sites near 28 ovarian genes (72 risk sites, 80 protective sites),14 CpG sites near 2 granulosa genes (PER3, RUNX3) (7 risk sites, 7 protective sites) were associated with menopausal age. PDCD6IP is a protective factor at both gene and protein levels, while INPP5B exhibits protective effects at both methylation and protein levels. PRKCZ and SKI show consistent risk or protective effects at both methylation and expression levels. Ovarian genes, 24 eQTL genes (e.g., PITPNM2, PPP2R3A), 3 pQTL genes (e.g., IFI16), and 4 methylation sites exhibited co-localization. Notably, IFI16 demonstrated high co-localization in both eQTL and pQTL analyses. Only HMBOX1 exhibited eQTL co-localization. Among PRKCB, IFI16, and other genes, enriched in neurogenesis, immune regulation, and insulin resistance pathways revealed close interactions. The IRF1 gene enriched in T cell activation and circadian rhythm has the strongest interaction. Ovarian genes (e.g., RPS8, IFI16) and granulosa cell genes (e.g., PEX6, GFPT2) exhibit significant eQTL signals in brain and intestinal tissues, supporting their tissue-specific regulatory functions. Limitations, reasons for caution The eQTL data were derived fromblood gene expression, not the native tissue specific data. Consequently, all the signals in blood may not fully represent the true exposure levels in target tissues, potentially leading to an underestimated association between instrumental variables and target exposures. Wider implications of the findings The potential mechanisms by which ovarian genes such as IFI16 and PDCD6IP regulate menopausal age through multi-level modulation at the methylation, gene expression, and protein levels, Ovarian aging is not determined solely by local factors but is rather driven by a cross-tissue genetic network involving the brain, gut, and ovaries. title: MULTI-OMICS PROFILING OF HUMAN HIPPOCAMPUS NEUROGENIC NICHE TO DECIPHER THE NEUROBIOLOGY OF MAJOR DEPRESSION
abstract: Abstract To investigate the presence of a neurogenic niche in human adult hippocampus and the molecular basis of smaller dentate gyrus (DG) in Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), we applied single-nucleus RNA (snRNA- seq) and accessible chromatin sequencing (snATAC-seq), together with spatial RNA sequencing (Visium, 10x Genomics). We assayed the hippocampus proper from 9 neurotypical (age 40 ± 12 yrs.) and 7 untreated MDD (age 48 ± 10 yrs.) males (2-3 biological replicates). A subsample (3 MDDs; 3 neurotypicals) were used for Visium (2 biological replicates, 12 capture areas total). Samples had RIN ³ 7 (7.9 ± 0.4). Libraries were sequenced (NovaSeq 6000 Sequencer, Illumina) to 62,000 reads/cell for RNA libraries, 33,000 reads/cell for ATAC libraries, and 67,000 reads/spot for Visium libraries (total 41,878 spots). RNA and ATAC data were preprocessed using Seurat, Signac, and DoubletFinder, batch effects removed using Harmony. Multimodal data for 293,236 cells were integrated using Weighted Nearest Neighbor analysis in Seurat, cell types annotated using canonical gene expression, enriched genes identified by a Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Bonferroni-adjusted p-value), and prediction scores from integration with spatial data implemented with TransferData function in Seurat. Gene ontology (GO) terms were generated using clusterProfiler (FDR-adjusted q-value). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in MDDs vs. neurotypicals, were identified using a mixed linear model implemented in limma with a pseudobulk approach, we aggregated count matrix across sample and cluster, and used a random effect to control for multiple samples/donor and fixed effects for age, PMI, and batch. We identified hippocampus canonical cell types: granule neurons (GN), non-granule excitatory neurons (ExN), inhibitory neurons (InN), astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, vasculature, ciliated epithelial cells, choroid plexus, Cajal-Retzius, and oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPc). We discovered: a neural progenitor cell cluster (NPC) enriched for EGFR (p = 1.68E-35), BMPR1B (p = 1.25E-31), NOTCH2 (p = 4.43E-11), and DLL3 (p = 4.48E-21), with top GO terms ‘nervous system development’ (q=2.11E-05) and ‘cell fate commitment’ (q = 2.11E-05); and immature granule neurons (ImN) enriched for PROX1, DCX, CALB2 (p <2.23E-308), that expressed GAD1 (p <2.23E-308),with GO terms ‘neuron axonogenesis’ (q = 9.11E-05), ‘excitatory synapse assembly’ (q = 0.004), and ‘ephrin receptor signaling pathway’ (q = 0.024). ATAC showed NPC and ImN had increased chromatin accessibility of ASCL1, involved in neuronal commitment (p = 0.00013) and differentiation (p <2.23E-308). Visium confirmed the expected anatomical location of canonical cell clusters, and mapped NPCs and ImNs to the DG region. In MDD vs. neurotypicals, DEGs included: upregulated interferon inducible genes (IFI44, IFI6, IFIT1, etc.) in GN, ExN, InN, ImN, astrocyte, microglia, choroid plexus, OPC (p <0.01), and downregulated transthyretin (TTR), which transports thyroid hormone, in GN, ExN, InN, astrocyte, microglia, vasculature, and ciliated epithelial cells (p <4.06E-05). This first single cell and spatial multiome study of human adult hippocampus reveals a neurogenic niche and supports a role of neuroinflammation in MDD. GAD1 expression in ImN explains their known inhibition of mature GNs. Molecular landscape of DEGs in MDD cell population points to druggable targets for MDD. title: IL-15—Driven NK-like Activation Is Augmented in Senescent CD57+CD8+ Memory T Cells 2255278
abstract: IL-15 can stimulate CD8+ memory T (Tm) cells to exert NKG2D-mediated NK-like cytotoxicity in a TCR-independent manner, which can contribute to immunopathological host injury during viral infections. However, it has not been fully elucidated if senescent status of CD8+ Tm cells determines the degree of IL-15—induced NK-like activation. Here, we examined IL-15 responsiveness of replicative-senescent CD57+CD8+ Tm cells compared to CD57-CD8+ Tm cells and investigated the underlying molecular mechanism. We obtained PBMCs from healthy donors (20-74 years) and analyzed CD57+CD8+ and CD57-CD8+ Tm cells by flow cytometry and bulk RNA-seq following ex vivo IL-15 stimulation. In addition, we performed single nucleus-multiome analysis (snRNA/ATAC-seq) of CD57+CD8+ and CD57-CD8+ Tm cells. We further analyzed single-cell transcriptomes of bystander CD8+ T cells identified with dCODE MHC-I multimers from PBMCs of patients with acute HAV infection. We demonstrated that senescent CD57+CD8+ Tm cells exhibit augmented IL-15—induced NK-like activation compared to non-senescent CD57-CD8+ Tm cells. The degree of IL-15—induced NK-like cytotoxicity was correlated with age and the proportion of CD57+CD8+ Tm cells. Furthermore, CD57+CD8+ Tm cells exhibited stronger NK-like activation than CD57- counterparts in patients with acute HAV infection, where the NK-like bystander activation of memory CD8+ T cells is well-exemplified. Notably, CD57+CD8+ Tm cells exhibited upregulation of Aiolos, known as a key regulator of AP-1 that is critical for IL-15—induced NK-like activation of CD8+ Tm cells. Our findings reveal a mechanism by which augmented IL-15—induced NK-like activation of senescent CD57+CD8+ Tm cells is associated with enhanced bystander activation of CD8+ T cells in the elderly, providing insights for novel molecular targets for the treatment of aging-associated immunopathology. n/a Immune Response Regulation: Cellular Mechanisms (IRC)

title: Unlocking heart anti-aging potential: the SIRT2-STAT3-CDKN2B pathway as a bridge between fiction and reality
abstract: As the global aging population continues to expand, the impact of age-related cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) on health and longevity has garnered increasing concern. According to data from the World Health Organization, CVDs accounted for an estimated 17.9 million global deaths in 2019, constituting 32% of all worldwide mortality. Consequently, there is a pressing need to delve into the molecular underpinnings of cardiac aging to pave the way for future advancements in preventive and therapeutic approaches. Sirtuins, known as silent information regulator 2 proteins, constitute a family of histone deacetylases (HDACs) responsible for catalyzing the deacetylation of both histone and non-histone lysine residues. Beyond their deacetylase activity, certain sirtuins also exhibit adenosine diphosphate (ADP)-ribozyme, demalonylase, desuccinylase, or glutarylase properties [1]. Among the Sirtuin family, SIRT2, situated in the cytosol, remains relatively less explored. It was found expression in a broad spectrum of tissues, with a prominent presence in metabolism-related tissues, such as the heart, brain, and adipose tissue. SIRT2 plays a pivotal role in various metabolic processes. Over the past years, researchers have unveiled its significant contributions to cardiovascular diseases. For instance, SIRT2 functions as a cardioprotective deacetylase, guarding against aging-dependent and Ang II-induced pathological hypertrophy by sustaining cardiac LKB1-AMPK signaling. Comparatively, SIRT2-knockout mice, in contrast to their wild-type counterparts, displayed exacerbated cardiac hypertrophy, fibrosis, and compromised cardiac function following angiotensin II infusion. These findings underscore the potential of SIRT2 as a therapeutic target for addressing pathological cardiac hypertrophy [2]. Furthermore, SIRT2 has been implicated in age-dependent vascular aging. As individuals age, both SIRT2 protein levels and its activity tend to diminish, and the deficiency of SIRT2 exacerbates vascular dysfunction and remodeling in elderly mice. Researchers have elucidated that SIRT2 contributes to the regulation of vascular aging, in part, by inhibiting the aging-associated protein, p66Shc, and its downstream mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mROS). This discovery unveils an unforeseen role for the deacetylase SIRT2 as a guardian against vascular aging and underscores the significance of the cytoplasm-mitochondria axis involving SIRT2-p66Shc-mROS in the context of age-induced vascular remodeling [3]. SIRT2 also plays a vital role in peripheral neurological diseases. Wild-type GARS binds to SIRT2, inhibiting its deacetylation activity and leading to increased acetylated α-tubulin levels, a major SIRT2 substrate. The catalytic domain of GARS, frequently associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2D (CMT2D) mutations, interacts closely with SIRT2. However, CMT2D mutations in GARS fail to inhibit SIRT2 deacetylation, resulting in decreased acetylated α-tubulin levels. Reducing SIRT2 genetically in a Drosophila model has been effective in mitigating GARS-induced axonal CMT neuropathy and extending lifespan, offering a potential treatment avenue for hereditary peripheral nerve diseases [4]. Nonetheless, all of the aforementioned studies were conducted in non-primate models. This raises the question of the molecular mechanisms underlying cardiac pathophysiological changes induced by aging in primates. In a groundbreaking study led by Guang-Hui Liu’s team [5], a milestone was reached as they conducted a comprehensive analysis of the transcriptome and proteome of aging hearts in cynomolgus monkeys. For the first time, this research unveiled the pivotal biological pathway driving cardiac aging in primates, namely the SIRT2-STAT3-CDKN2B pathway. This discovery fills a critical gap in our understanding of age-related cardiac physiological changes in primates. Moreover, the study demonstrated the potential of reversing age-related heart dysfunction through SIRT2 gene therapy (Fig. 1). The role of SIRT2 in cardiac aging. (Contributed by Jingxuan Liu) In this study, researchers employed a naturally aging model using cynomolgus monkeys. They systematically investigated aging-related phenotypes, including cardiac hypertrophy, sarcomeric abnormalities, and inflammation. Their approach encompassed high-throughput proteome and transcriptome sequencing, gene editing techniques, experimentation with human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes, gene expression modulation, and the application of viral vectors for gene therapy. Their findings pointed to a crucial factor in primate cardiomyocyte aging: the down-regulation of SIRT2 protein expression. Initially, the researchers conducted a comprehensive analysis to identify aging-associated proteins. Remarkably, they found that the deacetylase SIRT2 was the sole protein exhibiting down-regulation during aging, and it was linked to both various cardiovascular diseases and epigenetic regulation. This discovery emerged from a joint analysis that encompassed differential senescence proteins discovered in cynomolgus monkey hearts and distinct sets of protein-coding genes. These gene sets included those related to senescence-related cardiovascular diseases, Aging Atlas senescence-related genes, and genes associated with epigenetic regulation. Furthermore, the researchers made a groundbreaking advancement by generating SIRT2-deficient human cardiomyocytes using CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene editing, alongside human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes. This pioneering approach revealed that SIRT2-deficient human cardiomyocytes displayed a range of cardiac senescence-related characteristics, such as accelerated senescence and abnormal hypertrophy. Importantly, their gene expression profiles closely mirrored those observed in the aging hearts of cynomolgus monkeys. Next, the researchers delved deeper into the mechanisms underlying their findings through a combination of advanced techniques. They conducted a comprehensive analysis that included transcription factor network analysis, immunoprecipitation coupled with protein profiling, protein-targeted mutagenesis, chromatin immunoprecipitation, real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction, and in situ electron microscopy. Their investigations unveiled a significant interaction between the SIRT2 protein and the transcription factor STAT3. This interaction prompted the deacetylation of STAT3 at K685, subsequently inhibiting the transcription and expression of the cell cycle-arresting gene CDKN2B. The absence of SIRT2 led to an increase in the acetylation level of STAT3 in human cardiomyocytes, resulting in the upregulation of the CDKN2B gene and, consequently, cardiomyocyte senescence and hypertrophy. In contrast, both the overexpression of SIRT2 and the knockdown of CDKN2B exhibited the ability to delay the senescence of human cardiomyocytes. Having established that SIRT2 plays a pivotal role in regulating human myocardial senescence, the researchers hypothesized that gene therapies centered around SIRT2 could potentially delay cardiac senescence. To investigate this hypothesis, they conducted an experiment where they introduced lentiviruses carrying SIRT2 proteins into the myocardium of 24-month-old mice at multiple sites. Remarkably, after just 2 weeks, they observed substantial improvements in key cardiac parameters, including ejection fraction, fractional shortening, and the extent of cardiac hypertrophy in the aged mice. These findings suggest that SIRT2 holds significant promise as a critical target for in vivo interventions aimed at combating myocardial aging. While this research has yielded exciting breakthrough results, there are avenues for further exploration and refinement: (i) Species differences: Future research should consider other primate models or conduct clinical studies in humans to better understand human heart aging. (ii) Mechanism analysis: Further study is needed to delve into the molecular interactions and regulation of the SIRT2-STAT3-CDKN2B pathway. (iii) Clinical challenges: Challenges in translating findings to clinical treatments require validation through clinical trials for effectiveness and safety. In conclusion, this study identifies the SIRT2-STAT3-CDKN2B pathway as a key regulator of senescence in primate cardiomyocytes. This discovery advances our understanding of cardiac aging and offers potential therapeutic targets. The down-regulation of SIRT2 may serve as a biomarker of cardiac senescence, which may help to accurately assess the functional status of the heart and predict the risk of cardiac senescence-associated diseases and may lead to the development of individualized interventions to prevent and control diseases. Future research may lead to interventions and treatments, such as SIRT2-enhanced gene therapies or SIRT2-specific agonists, with the potential to extend a healthy lifespan and address cardiovascular diseases. title: SIRT7 mediates L1 elements transcriptional repression and their association with the nuclear lamina.
abstract: Long interspersed elements-1 (LINE-1, L1) are retrotransposons that hold the capacity of self-propagation in the genome with potential mutagenic outcomes. How somatic cells restrict L1 activity and how this process becomes dysfunctional during aging and in cancer cells is poorly understood. L1s are enriched at lamin-associated domains, heterochromatic regions of the nuclear periphery. Whether this association is necessary for their repression has been elusive. Here we show that the sirtuin family member SIRT7 participates in the epigenetic transcriptional repression of L1 genome-wide in both mouse and human cells. SIRT7 depletion leads to increased L1 expression and retrotransposition. Mechanistically, we identify a novel interplay between SIRT7 and Lamin A/C in L1 repression. Our results demonstrate that SIRT7-mediated H3K18 deacetylation regulates L1 expression and promotes L1 association with elements of the nuclear lamina. The failure of such activity might contribute to the observed genome instability and compromised viability in SIRT7 knockout mice. Overall, our results reveal a novel function of SIRT7 on chromatin organization by mediating the anchoring of L1 to the nuclear envelope, and a new functional link of the nuclear lamina with transcriptional repression.
